viva.lesson:
How do you know that circulation has returned? There are three signs.

A palpable pulse, with a measurable blood pressure. An abrupt, sustained rise in the end-tidal carbon dioxide, typically to forty millimetres of mercury or more. And spontaneous arterial pressure waves on the arterial line, appearing between or without compressions.

[[Return of circulation: a pulse and a blood pressure, an abrupt sustained rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide, and spontaneous waves on the arterial line.]]

Two points of precision. The figure of forty is the wording on the algorithm. The guideline text itself speaks of a sudden rise of more than ten millimetres of mercury. Give both if you're pressed.

And the practical rule. The rise is a strong hint, not a licence to stop. Don't interrupt compressions the moment the number jumps. Carry on to the planned rhythm check, and confirm it there.

And the last role is the most dangerous one. Can a low value tell you to stop?

p12.question: Drugs, access, causes and when to stop
p12.bridge: Those are the rules for the ordinary arrest. Some arrests break them. Section four is about those.
p12.lesson:
Sometimes nothing works. Then the question is who may stop, and on what grounds, without relying on one person's feeling in the back of an ambulance. The answer is a set of termination of resuscitation rules, built from registries of arrests outside hospital.

The one the Grand Tests have asked twice is the universal rule. It has three criteria, and all three must be present. The arrest was not witnessed by the EMS crew. No shock was delivered at any point. And there was no return of spontaneous circulation.

Look at what those three say together. Nobody professional saw the collapse, so it had already lasted an unknown time. The rhythm was never shockable, so it was never the kind that responds best. And nothing has worked. Survival in that group is very low.

[[Universal termination rule, all three: arrest not witnessed by EMS, no shock delivered, no ROSC. It is the rule for a tiered EMS system with both basic and advanced crews.]]

Which rule applies depends on what the crew is allowed to do. The basic life support rule uses the same three criteria. The advanced life support rule adds two more: the arrest was not witnessed by a bystander, and no bystander gave CPR. So it is the stricter rule, because an advanced crew can offer more. A note on your card had this backwards. For the exam, hold on to one line: a tiered system with both kinds of crew uses the universal rule.

Now the measurement that must not be used alone, and it is the trap in this card. You saw that a low end-tidal carbon dioxide means poor flow. It is tempting to turn that into a stopping rule. The guideline allows it only in a narrow form. In an intubated patient, an end-tidal that has failed to rise above ten millimetres of mercury after twenty minutes of advanced life support may be one part of a wider judgement. In a patient who is not intubated, no end-tidal cut-off should be used at all, because a leaking mask makes the number unreliable.

[[End-tidal carbon dioxide is never used alone to stop a resuscitation. Under ten after twenty minutes counts only in an intubated patient, and only as one factor among several.]]

When a rule is met, crews should be prepared to stop at the scene, and they need training in telling a family about a death. Transporting a patient with CPR in progress is dangerous for the crew and seldom saves anyone who meets the rule.

One boundary. These rules were built for medical arrests outside hospital. They are not validated for trauma, for overdose, or for arrests in hospital. Trauma has its own logic, and Marrow asked it. A resuscitative thoracotomy is for penetrating trauma with less than about fifteen minutes of CPR, or blunt trauma with less than about ten. A man with a penetrating chest wound in asystole after twenty-five minutes is outside that window. The answer is an echo, and with no cardiac motion, to stop.

viva.question: What is the role of end-tidal CO2 during CPR?
viva.lesson:
For ambulance crews there's the universal termination of resuscitation rule. All three criteria must be present. The arrest was not witnessed by the crew. No shock was delivered. And there was no return of circulation. If any one is missing, they continue and transport. It's reasonable in a tiered system with basic and advanced crews, who should be prepared to stop on scene.

Where does the end-tidal fit in? The evidence began with Levine, in the New England Journal in nineteen ninety-seven. A hundred and fifty patients with PEA outside hospital. After twenty minutes of advanced life support, the average end-tidal was four point four millimetres of mercury in those who died, against thirty-two point eight in those who survived to hospital admission. A later review of seventeen studies found that a value below ten at twenty minutes gave about half a percent chance of return of circulation.

That sounds decisive. It isn't. The number is confounded, by adrenaline, bicarbonate, ventilation, a leak, and the cause of the arrest. And the evidence is of low quality.

[[End-tidal carbon dioxide is never used alone to stop. In an intubated patient, failure to rise above ten after twenty minutes may be one part of a multimodal decision.]]

And there's a stronger line. In a patient who is not intubated, no cut-off should be used at any time. The guideline classes that as harm.

So when the professor asks, what value means stop, the answer is that no single value does.

p12.question: Special arrests: pregnancy, asthma, poisoning, ECPR
p12.bridge: Displacement and an expert airway are the two priorities. The algorithm adds a short list of further changes.
p12.lesson:
Compressions push forward only what has returned to the heart. Now put a uterus on the inferior vena cava.

From about twenty weeks, when the fundus reaches the umbilicus, a woman lying flat has her vena cava and her aorta compressed by the uterus. Much of the venous return from the lower body never reaches the heart. You can compress perfectly, and there is little in the ventricle to move. So maternal arrest has two priorities instead of one: high-quality CPR, and relief of aortocaval compression.

The relief is manual. Someone pushes or pulls the uterus up and to the left, continuously, while the woman stays flat on her back. Why not tilt her on a wedge, as was done before? Because a tilted chest takes the force out of the compressions. Manual left uterine displacement keeps her flat for good compressions and still lifts the uterus off the cava.

[[In maternal arrest, from about twenty weeks, add continuous manual left uterine displacement with the woman flat. Tilting her weakens compressions. This is the most critical change to standard life support.]]

The bank asked it at twenty-eight weeks, and ninety-seven per cent got it. NEET's own version is subtler: why is a second rescuer essential in maternal arrest? For uterine displacement. The wrong options are 'for the caesarean' and 'for defibrillation'. The second pair of hands is holding the uterus.

Now the airway, and why it is worse here. The mucosa is swollen, so the view is poor and it bleeds. The stomach is full, and the sphincter above it is lax, so she aspirates easily. Her reserve of oxygen in the lungs is smaller and she uses oxygen faster, so she desaturates quickly. So a difficult airway is common, and the most experienced person available should manage it.

Which device? The bank asked for the preferred airway in maternal arrest, and ninety-two per cent chose the endotracheal tube, because a cuffed tube protects best against aspiration. A supraglottic airway is the alternative. Either is confirmed with waveform capnography. Once it is in, the rate is what you already know: one breath every six seconds with continuous compressions.

Two wrong options to recognise. 'Half-dose adrenaline in pregnancy' is wrong, because the doses don't change. 'Avoid intubation until ROSC' is wrong, because the airway is secured early.

And the team is larger from the first minute: obstetrics, the neonatal team, anaesthesia, intensive care. You'll see why two cards from now.

viva.question: How do you manage cardiac arrest in pregnancy?
viva.bridge: Good CPR plus continuous manual left uterine displacement, with an expert on the airway. Next: the full maternal and obstetric checklist →
viva.lesson:
Two priorities, of equal rank. High-quality CPR. And relief of aortocaval compression.

The first is exactly what you'd do for anyone.

The second is the pair of hands. Continuous manual left lateral uterine displacement. Continuous means someone is assigned to it and does nothing else. They move the uterus towards her left side, up and off the vessels, for as long as the arrest lasts.

[[The two priorities in maternal arrest are high-quality CPR and continuous manual left uterine displacement.]]

Then the airway, and here you're the right person in the room. A difficult airway is common in pregnancy. The mucosa is swollen and bleeds easily. The stomach behaves as if it's full. And, as we've just seen, she desaturates fast. So there's less room and less time. The guideline's answer is simple: use the most experienced provider. A tracheal tube, or a supraglottic airway if that's what gets oxygen in. And waveform capnography, to confirm the placement and to keep monitoring it.

Once the advanced airway is in, compressions run continuously and you give one breath every six seconds. Ten a minute. Not more. The temptation is to ventilate fast. But every extra breath raises the pressure in the chest and takes away a little more venous return, in a patient whose venous return is already the problem.

And the last line of the card is about people. Maternal arrest needs team planning in advance: obstetric, neonatal, emergency, anaesthesia, intensive care and the cardiac arrest service. One call should bring all of them, because in five minutes there's no time to make six calls.

Those are the principles. Now the checklist that sits under them.

p12.question: Special arrests: pregnancy, asthma, poisoning, ECPR
p12.bridge: If displacement, calcium and blood haven't restored a pulse, one obstacle remains, and it can be removed.
p12.lesson:
The maternal algorithm adds a short list to standard life support. Take the maternal changes first, then the obstetric ones, then the causes.

First, where the cannula goes. With the cava compressed, a drug injected into a leg vein may sit below the obstruction and never reach the heart. So access is placed above the diaphragm, in an arm, or intraosseous in the humerus.

Second, oxygen at a hundred per cent, and no excessive ventilation, for the reasons you know.

Third, magnesium. Many of these women are on a magnesium infusion for pre-eclampsia. Magnesium in excess abolishes the reflexes, depresses breathing, blocks conduction and stops the heart. So in a woman who arrests on a magnesium infusion, you stop the infusion and give calcium, as the chloride or the gluconate, which opposes magnesium at the cell membrane.

[[A woman who arrests while on a magnesium infusion: stop the magnesium and give intravenous calcium. Before the arrest magnesium is the treatment; during it, magnesium is a suspect.]]

The bank has three questions on this, and you need to keep them apart.

One: a pregnant woman in the ICU becomes bradycardic and then arrests. Which electrolyte? Hypermagnesaemia. Sixty-one per cent got it. The wrong options were low potassium and high calcium.

Two: arrest on intravenous magnesium for pre-eclampsia, with CPR and displacement already under way. Next step? Stop the magnesium and give calcium.

Three is different. Earlier you met the eclamptic woman who was seizing and went into VF, and the key gave magnesium with amiodarone. So here is the rule. If she was already receiving magnesium when she arrested, the answer is calcium. If she is eclamptic and has not been loaded, magnesium appears in the keyed answer.

Now the obstetric changes. There are three: continuous uterine displacement, detaching the fetal monitors, and preparing for delivery. Why take the monitors off? They get in the way of defibrillation and of the move to delivery, and they tell you nothing you can act on. The fetus is best served by getting the mother's circulation back. Marrow asked which step is not indicated in maternal arrest, and the answer was attaching fetal monitors.

Last, the causes, as an alphabet from A to H. Anaesthetic complications. Bleeding. Cardiovascular. Drugs. Embolic. Fever. General causes, which are the ordinary H's and T's. And hypertension.

{{**Maternal arrest: causes A–H**
**A**naesthetic complications • **B**leeding • **C**ardiovascular • **D**rugs (magnesium, local anaesthetic) • **E**mbolic (amniotic fluid, pulmonary) • **F**ever • **G**eneral H's and T's • **H**ypertension}}

One of them outweighs the rest. Obstetric haemorrhage is the commonest single cause of maternal arrest. So the bank's question, the commonest reversible cause of PEA in pregnancy, is answered by hypovolaemia from haemorrhage. That means wide lines above the diaphragm, a massive transfusion, drugs to contract the uterus, and the obstetrician. Eclampsia on its own seldom stops the heart.

[[PEA in pregnancy is hypovolaemia from obstetric haemorrhage until proved otherwise. Access goes above the diaphragm, and the fetal monitors come off.]]

viva.question: How do you manage cardiac arrest in pregnancy?
viva.bridge: IV above the diaphragm, stop magnesium and give calcium, detach monitors, think causes A to H. Next: when and why to deliver →
viva.lesson:
The algorithm sorts the tasks into two columns. Things done for the mother, and obstetric things.

The maternal column has four. Manage the airway. Give one hundred percent oxygen and avoid excess ventilation. Place the IV above the diaphragm. And if she's receiving IV magnesium, stop it and give calcium.

Take the IV first. Why above the diaphragm? Follow a drug from a femoral line. It enters the vena cava below the uterus, and that's the very vessel that's compressed. The adrenaline goes nowhere. [[In maternal arrest the IV goes above the diaphragm, because the gravid uterus obstructs venous return from below it.]] So an arm, or the neck, or the humerus if you need intraosseous access.

Now magnesium. Think who's on a magnesium infusion: the woman with pre-eclampsia or eclampsia. Magnesium in excess depresses breathing and the heart. It's the classic iatrogenic cause of arrest around delivery. So you stop the infusion and give its antagonist, calcium chloride or calcium gluconate. You've just used calcium against potassium. The same drug, against a different ion.

The obstetric column has three. Continuous lateral uterine displacement. Detach the fetal monitors. And prepare for resuscitative delivery. The monitors come off because they get in the way and add nothing you'd act on. During the arrest, the fetus is helped by one thing only: the mother's circulation.

And then the causes. The algorithm gives eight, A to H.

{{**Causes of maternal arrest, A–H**
**A** Anaesthetic complications · **B** Bleeding · **C** Cardiovascular · **D** Drugs
**E** Embolic · **F** Fever · **G** General (Hs and Ts) · **H** Hypertension}}

Anaesthetic complications: a high spinal, a failed airway, local anaesthetic toxicity. Those are yours. Bleeding. Cardiovascular. Drugs, with magnesium at the top. Embolic: clot, or amniotic fluid. Fever, meaning sepsis. General, the ordinary Hs and Ts. And hypertension, meaning pre-eclampsia and eclampsia.

So the hands are on the uterus, the line is in the arm, the causes are being thought through. And the clock is running. What happens at five minutes?

p12.question: Special arrests: pregnancy, asthma, poisoning, ECPR
p12.bridge: That was an obstacle to filling. The next arrests are defeated by gas and by temperature.
p12.lesson:
You have pushed the uterus aside by hand. If that isn't enough, you empty it.

Start with the name, because it changed in twenty twenty-five. What used to be called perimortem caesarean delivery is now resuscitative delivery. The old name suggested an operation done at the point of death to rescue the baby. The new one says what it is: a step in the mother's resuscitation. Emptying the uterus releases the vena cava, returns blood from the uterine circulation to hers, and makes her chest easier to compress and to ventilate. In the case series, the mother's pulse often came back just after delivery.

Now the clock. Preparation begins the moment the arrest is recognised. That is why the obstetric and neonatal teams were called in the first minute. The goal is delivery completed by five minutes, if there is no ROSC, in a woman whose fundus is at or above the umbilicus.

[[Resuscitative delivery, the new name for perimortem caesarean: prepare when the arrest is recognised, and complete delivery by five minutes if there is no ROSC. It is done to resuscitate the mother.]]

Where does five minutes come from? From Katz, Dotters and Droegemueller in nineteen eighty-six. They reasoned that the brain tolerates about four to five minutes without flow, so they proposed starting the operation at four minutes and delivering by five. That is the four-minute rule. It is a goal drawn from case reports, and the reviews that followed, by Katz in two thousand and five and Einav in twenty twelve, were case series as well. There has never been a randomised trial.

The bank tests this three ways. Timing at thirty-four weeks: within five minutes of the arrest if there is no ROSC. Ninety-two per cent. The wrong options are 'after twenty minutes of failed CPR', 'only after fetal death' and 'after ROSC'.

The origin of the four-minute rule: Katz. Fifty-four per cent.

And one question with a bad key, which only fourteen per cent matched. It asked which trial studied maternal arrest and perimortem caesarean, and the key was something called the HELP trial. No such trial exists. If Katz or a case series is among the options, choose it. If the same options return, eliminate the ones you can identify. MOMS was fetal surgery for spina bifida. ALPS, in obstetrics, was steroids for late preterm birth. PROWESS was a sepsis drug. What is left is the key.

The operation is done where she lies, with CPR and displacement continuing. You don't move her to theatre. The bank asked the incision, and only forty-five per cent knew it. It is a vertical midline incision from just above the pubic symphysis up to the umbilicus, because that is the fastest and gives the widest view, and then a vertical cut in the uterus. The wrong options begin above the umbilicus or at the xiphoid, and those miss the uterus.

[[Resuscitative delivery is done at the bedside during CPR, through a vertical midline incision from just above the symphysis pubis to the umbilicus.]]

Two more recommendations from twenty twenty-five. If she doesn't respond to standard resuscitation, extracorporeal CPR is reasonable. These are young patients with reversible causes, and in the reported series most of them survived. And for suspected amniotic fluid embolism, where sudden collapse with right heart failure is followed by consumptive coagulopathy and torrential bleeding, use a massive transfusion protocol with a balanced ratio of products, together with tranexamic acid.

You met this card in maternal arrest, and here's what matters for this question. If she arrests and the fundus is at or above the umbilicus, you prepare for resuscitative delivery from the moment of recognition, and complete it by five minutes.

This card also carries the twenty twenty-five line for suspected life-threatening amniotic fluid embolism: a balanced massive transfusion protocol together with tranexamic acid, both class one, with extracorporeal CPR reasonable if she doesn't respond. viva.question: How do you manage cardiac arrest in pregnancy?
viva.lesson:
This is the centre of the question.

The twenty twenty-five term is resuscitative delivery. It replaces perimortem caesarean delivery. And the change isn't cosmetic. Perimortem framed it as salvaging a fetus from a mother who is dying. Resuscitative names it for what it is: a manoeuvre in her resuscitation.

When do you prepare? At the recognition of cardiac arrest. Not at four minutes. From the first minute, someone is finding a scalpel and someone is calling the obstetric and neonatal teams.

And the goal. [[If the fundus is at or above the umbilicus and circulation has not returned, complete the delivery by five minutes, at the place where she arrested.]]

Why does emptying the uterus help her? Go back to the opening. The uterus was resting on the vena cava and the aorta. Deliver, and that compression is relieved more completely than any pair of hands can manage. Venous return comes back. Suddenly the compressions have something to work with. That's the card's point: emptying the uterus makes CPR effective.

Why five minutes? Because of the short reserve you learned two cards ago. And because CPR against a compressed vena cava was never giving much flow.

And why where she lies? Because moving her to theatre costs minutes and interrupts compressions. A scalpel is enough. CPR continues throughout, and so does the displacement, until the baby is out.

Now the point the panel tests. Is this done only if the baby is viable? No. [[Resuscitative delivery is done for the mother, whether or not the fetus is viable. It improves both maternal and fetal outcomes.]] If the fundus is at the umbilicus, the uterus obstructs, and the indication stands.

Two further twenty twenty-five recommendations sit on this card. First, extracorporeal CPR is reasonable in pregnant or peripartum patients who aren't responding to standard resuscitation. The reported survival after arrest is fifty-five percent in the ELSO registry, and eighty-seven percent of fifty-seven patients in a systematic review. Small numbers, and selected patients, but high.

Second, for suspected life-threatening amniotic fluid embolism: a massive transfusion protocol with a balanced strategy, together with tranexamic acid. Both are class one. Keep that in your pocket. You'll need it in the next lesson.

p12.question: Special arrests: pregnancy, asthma, poisoning, ECPR
p12.bridge: Extracorporeal rewarming is the top of a ladder. The bank asks the rungs below it, and the rules for a cold arrest.
p12.lesson:
Three conditions share this card because the guideline of twenty twenty-five gave each a physical answer.

First, asthma. Life-threatening asthma doesn't kill through damaged lung. It kills through gas that can't get out. Each breath stacks on the one before, the chest over-inflates, the pressure inside rises, and venous return is squeezed off. So in an asthmatic who arrests on a ventilator, think of two things at once: breath stacking, relieved by disconnecting the circuit briefly and letting the chest empty, and a tension pneumothorax. When the bronchospasm itself won't yield to standard treatment, two rescues are named. Extracorporeal life support may be reasonable, because it takes over gas exchange and buys time for the bronchodilators. And volatile anaesthetics may be considered, because they relax bronchial smooth muscle directly. Survival in the observational series is high, eighty-three to a hundred per cent, because the disease is reversible.

Second, heat. Heat stroke is a core temperature above forty degrees with brain dysfunction. The injury to cells depends on how long they stay above the critical temperature. So the only thing that matters is the speed at which the core falls.

Water carries heat away far faster than air. So the preferred method is immersion in ice water, at one to five degrees. The target is to cool as fast as possible, at a rate of at least nought point one five of a degree per minute. If ice water isn't available, tepid water or ice water held in a tarpaulin is the next choice. Evaporative cooling with ice packs is the fallback when immersion is impossible.

[[Heat stroke: immersion in ice water, cooling at least nought point one five of a degree per minute, and stop at about thirty-eight point six degrees. Antipyretics and dantrolene do nothing.]]

Why do antipyretics fail? Because this isn't fever. In fever the hypothalamus has raised its set-point, and paracetamol lowers it. In heat stroke the set-point is normal and the body simply can't shed the heat. Dantrolene belongs to malignant hyperthermia only.

The bank asked the first step twice. A hot day, a core of forty-one, confusion: ice-water immersion. The wrong options were cooling blankets with fans, and cold intravenous fluid alone.

And here is the wrong key. A question on exertional heat stroke was keyed 'cool to at least thirty-six degrees to prevent rebound', and seventy-eight per cent chose it. That is too far. You stop active cooling at about thirty-eight point six to thirty-nine, because the core goes on falling after the patient leaves the water. If 'stop at thirty-nine' is offered, choose it.

Third, cold, at its severe end. Below twenty-eight degrees the heart fibrillates easily and doesn't respond well to anything until it is warm. The best way to warm it is from the inside, with the circulation supported at the same time. So for a hypothermic arrest the recommendation is rewarming with extracorporeal life support. It may also be used for a core below twenty-eight degrees even without an arrest.

Who should be offered it? Not everyone found cold is alive. The guideline says to use a prognostic score, HOPE or ICE, to decide. HOPE gives a probability of survival, and under ten per cent argues against starting.

[[Hypothermic arrest: rewarm with extracorporeal life support, with the HOPE or ICE score guiding who is cannulated. A core below twenty-eight degrees can be rewarmed this way even without arrest.]]

viva.lesson:
Now the numbers. This card is the AHA's twenty twenty-five line on life-threatening hyperthermia, and there are three numbers to own.

First, the water. Ice water, at one to five degrees Celsius, is preferred over the other methods.

Second, the rate. At least zero point one five degrees per minute. Make that real. It's one degree every six or seven minutes. Our man starts at forty-one point five and has about three degrees to lose, so at the minimum rate that's roughly twenty minutes. The SCCM gives you the cross-check: below thirty-nine within thirty minutes. And the Wilderness Medical Society quotes ice water at about zero point two degrees per minute, against zero point one one for wet towels in air.

{{pic}}

On your screen, that's the steep blue line against the shallow one.

Third, when to stop. This is the mock favourite, and most residents say thirty-seven. That's the trap.

Think about how you cooled him: from the outside in. By the time the core reads thirty-eight and a half, his skin and limbs are far colder than that. Lift him out, and heat keeps flowing from the warm core into that cold shell, and cold blood keeps returning from the limbs. So the core goes on falling after the cooling has ended. That's afterdrop, and you'll meet the same word in hypothermia.

Stop late, and he overshoots into hypothermia and starts to shiver. And shivering makes heat. So you take him out early, in the band shown in green, and let the drift finish the job. Keep the probe in, because the temperature can also rebound.

[[Key number: cool at zero point one five degrees per minute or faster, get below thirty-nine within thirty minutes, and stop at thirty-eight point three to thirty-eight point eight, because the core keeps falling after I stop.]]

viva.question: Classify accidental hypothermia and outline management, including when to use ECMO.

viva.lesson:
You met this card a few minutes ago in heatstroke, for ice-water immersion. Now read the row above it. For life-threatening hypothermia, the AHA in twenty twenty-five recommends extracorporeal life support for rewarming, with prognostic scores such as HOPE and ICE to decide who gets it. And it allows the circuit below twenty-eight degrees even without an arrest. Remember the note on that card as well: in hyperthermia, minutes of delay cost outcome, but hypothermia lowers demand and mimics death, and that's why you reach for a circuit instead of stopping early. The European guideline says the same, and differs mainly in the number of shocks.

[[Evidence: ERC twenty twenty-five: rewarm the arrested patient on VA-ECMO, selected by the HOPE score, not by potassium alone. AHA twenty twenty-five agrees, with one shock instead of three.]]

p12.question: Special arrests: pregnancy, asthma, poisoning, ECPR
p12.bridge: ECPR only helps if the cause can be fixed. The commonest fixable cause of an adult arrest is a blocked coronary.
p12.lesson:
Extracorporeal CPR means starting ECMO during an arrest that hasn't responded to conventional resuscitation. It doesn't treat anything. It replaces the circulation, so that the brain is perfused while somebody fixes the cause.

The configuration is always venoarterial. Think about why. In venovenous ECMO, oxygenated blood is returned to a vein and relies on the patient's own heart to send it round. This heart is still. Only blood returned to an artery perfuses anything.

[[ECPR is venoarterial ECMO, always, because there is no cardiac output to carry venous return forward. It buys time for a reversible cause; it does not treat one.]]

Who is a candidate? Every criterion answers one of two questions: was the brain without flow for only a short time, and is there something to fix? So: a witnessed arrest, with bystander CPR. An initial shockable rhythm, or another reversible cause. A younger patient with few other illnesses. And a definitive treatment standing ready: angioplasty, thrombectomy, rewarming.

The clock is the low-flow time, the time spent on conventional CPR. Most programmes aim to have the patient on the circuit within sixty minutes of the arrest.

The exclusions are the mirror image, plus three mechanical ones. An unwitnessed arrest. A long period with no CPR. A terminal illness. Then severe aortic regurgitation, because blood pumped backwards up the aorta pours through the leaking valve and distends the ventricle. Uncontrolled bleeding, because the circuit needs heparin. And aortic dissection.

What is the evidence? Three trials, and they disagree for a reason. ARREST, in Minneapolis, took thirty patients with refractory VF into a highly practised system, and survival to discharge was forty-three per cent against seven. It was stopped early. The Prague trial, with two hundred and sixty-four patients, found thirty-one per cent against twenty-two for good neurological survival, which was not significant. INCEPTION, across ten Dutch centres, found twenty against sixteen, also not significant. So the benefit appears only in fast, experienced systems, and the guideline calls ECPR reasonable in selected patients within a trained and equipped system.

Now the Grand Test question, which only forty-two per cent got right. It quoted the Surugadai criteria from Tokyo and asked which is not an exclusion. Four were offered: a presumed non-cardiac cause, ROSC within ten minutes of arrival, a core temperature under thirty-five degrees, and pregnancy. The answer is the core temperature under thirty-five. The true exclusion in those criteria is a core under thirty. A patient at thirty to thirty-five is mildly cold, and that is protective.

[[Surugadai ECPR exclusions: presumed non-cardiac cause, ROSC within ten minutes of arrival, core temperature below thirty degrees, and pregnancy. A core of thirty to thirty-five is not an exclusion.]]

Notice that ROSC within ten minutes is an exclusion and not a reason to cannulate. A patient who has a pulse no longer has a refractory arrest.

a The configuration used
b Who is a candidate
c The time target

card.a:
a **Venoarterial**, always - the patient has no cardiac output, so a venous return would circulate nothing.
b Refractory arrest with witnessed onset, bystander CPR, an initial shockable rhythm or another reversible cause, a younger patient with few comorbidities, and definitive treatment immediately available - PCI, thrombectomy, rewarming.

viva.question: What is ECPR and who is a candidate?
viva.bridge: ECPR is VA ECMO in refractory arrest, as a bridge to fixing a reversible cause. Next: the checklist that selects candidates →
viva.lesson:
ECPR is VA ECMO, started during CPR, in a refractory cardiac arrest. Always venoarterial. That's your definition, and the letters VA must be in it.

Now who gets it? Before the list, two terms that make the list obvious.

No-flow time is from collapse until someone starts compressions. Nothing is reaching the brain. Low-flow time is from the start of CPR until the pulse returns, or until the ECMO is running. The brain is getting a trickle.

The brain tolerates almost no no-flow, and only a limited amount of low-flow. Every selection criterion is a way of asking about one of those, or about the cause.

Witnessed arrest, with bystander CPR. That means the no-flow time was short. The brain was protected from the first minutes.

An initial shockable rhythm, or another reversible cause. That means there's something to fix. Fibrillation usually points to a coronary occlusion, and that can be opened.

A younger patient with few comorbidities. That means the reserve to survive what follows.

And definitive treatment immediately available. Angioplasty for the coronary. Thrombectomy for a pulmonary embolus. Rewarming for hypothermia.

[[The candidate: a witnessed, refractory arrest, with early bystander CPR, a shockable rhythm or a reversible cause, in a younger patient, with flow established within about sixty minutes.]]

The time target follows. Keep the low-flow time as short as you can. Most programmes aim to be on ECMO within sixty minutes of the arrest. And that means deciding early. Cannulation takes time. Many programmes make the call at ten to fifteen minutes of failed advanced life support. If you wait until forty minutes to think of it, you've already missed.

Then the exclusions, and each has a reason. An unwitnessed arrest, or a long time without CPR: the brain is already lost. A known terminal illness: there's no other bank for the bridge. Severe aortic regurgitation: the machine pumps backwards up the aorta, and a leaking valve lets that flow pour into the ventricle. And uncontrolled bleeding, because the circuit needs anticoagulation.

The word that carries the whole indication is reversible. ECPR without a reversible cause and a plan already in place is a bridge to nowhere.

So how does a team turn those principles into a decision at the bedside, in thirty seconds?

viva.question: Classify accidental hypothermia and outline management, including when to use ECMO.
viva.bridge: Venoarterial, for a reversible cause; hypothermia is the most reversible of all. Next: HOPE, potassium and the 6-hour rule →
viva.lesson:
So which circuit? This card is about extracorporeal CPR in general, and hypothermia turns out to be its best case.

The configuration is venoarterial, always. Think about why. A venovenous circuit takes blood from a vein, oxygenates it, and hands it back to the right heart, trusting the heart to send it on. In arrest there's no cardiac output. The blood has to be returned to an artery, because the circuit is now the pump as well as the lung.

And in hypothermia it does a third job. The circuit carries a heat exchanger, so the same machine that restores flow also rewarms. Flow and heat together. That's why the ERC prefers VA-ECMO, and prefers it over conventional bypass. It can also stay in place afterwards, if the heart and lungs are slow to recover.

Now look at the usual candidate on this card. A witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, a short low-flow time, cannulation within about sixty minutes. And the usual exclusions: unwitnessed arrest, a long time down.

Hypothermia bends those rules, and you should say why. The word carrying the indication on this card is reversible. Extracorporeal CPR buys time for a definitive treatment. Here the definitive treatment is rewarming, and the circuit delivers it. And the sixty-minute clock assumes a warm brain. A brain that cooled before the arrest runs on a different clock.

So for arrest, the decision is simple. He goes on venoarterial ECMO. The harder question is the patient who hasn't arrested yet, and how you choose. That's next.

[[What I do next: ECMO for arrest, or for instability: systolic below ninety, ventricular arrhythmia, or core below thirty. A HOPE score of ten percent or more supports it. Mechanical CPR for transport.]]

p12.question: After ROSC: the first hours
p12.bridge: Two of those five targets are set at the ventilator. Take them properly, starting with the lungs.
p12.lesson:
Five targets, and each one exists for the brain.

Blood pressure: a mean arterial pressure of at least sixty-five millimetres of mercury. After an arrest the brain loses its autoregulation. Normally it holds its own flow steady across a range of pressures. Now its flow simply follows the pressure. So hypotension is a second ischaemic injury.

Oxygen: a saturation of ninety to ninety-eight per cent, which is an arterial oxygen tension of sixty to a hundred and five. Too little repeats the injury. Too much feeds free-radical damage in tissue that has just been reperfused. And you keep a hundred per cent oxygen running until the oximeter gives a reading you can trust, and titrate down only then.

Carbon dioxide: an arterial tension of thirty-five to forty-five. Carbon dioxide sets the calibre of the brain's vessels. Low constricts them and cuts flow to a brain that is already short of it. High dilates them and raises intracranial pressure.

Temperature: deliberate temperature control for at least thirty-six hours in any patient who doesn't follow commands, at a goal anywhere from thirty-two to thirty-seven point five degrees. The next section is spent on why that range is so wide. For now hold one thing: the part that matters is preventing fever.

Angiography: before discharge, in survivors where a cardiac cause is suspected, especially after a shockable rhythm, with unexplained left ventricular dysfunction, or with severe ischaemia. That is the non-urgent indication. The urgent one comes three cards from now.

{{**After ROSC (AHA 2025)**
MAP | ≥65 mmHg
SpO₂ | 90–98% (PaO₂ 60–105 mmHg)
PaCO₂ | 35–45 mmHg
Temperature | 32–37.5 °C for ≥36 h, if not following commands
Glucose | avoid <70 and >180 mg/dL}}

[[After ROSC: mean arterial pressure at least sixty-five, saturation ninety to ninety-eight per cent, arterial carbon dioxide thirty-five to forty-five, and temperature control at thirty-two to thirty-seven point five degrees for at least thirty-six hours.]]

Now the trap that is built on history. A bank question asks for the target temperature after a VF arrest, and its key is thirty-two to thirty-four degrees. Only fifty-seven per cent chose it. That was the right answer from two thousand and two to about twenty ten. It isn't wrong inside today's range. It is just no longer the range. If thirty-two to thirty-seven point five, or fever prevention, is among the options, choose that. If only historical ranges are offered, thirty-two to thirty-four is the keyed one.

viva.bridge: MAP ≥65, SpO2 90-98%, PaCO2 35-45, temperature control ≥36 h. Next: who goes to the cath lab now →
viva.lesson:
This is a card of numbers, so I'll give them plainly. The reasons come in the next question.

{{**AHA 2025 targets after ROSC**
MAP ≥ 65 mmHg
SpO2 90–98% (PaO2 60–105 mmHg); 100% O2 until SpO2 is reliable
PaCO2 35–45 mmHg
Temperature control ≥ 36 h at 32–37.5 °C if not following commands}}

Blood pressure: a mean arterial pressure of at least sixty-five. Hypotension is to be avoided.

Oxygen: a hundred percent until the saturation can be measured reliably. Then titrate to an SpO2 of ninety to ninety-eight percent, which is a PaO2 of sixty to a hundred and five.

Carbon dioxide: a PaCO2 of thirty-five to forty-five. Normal.

Temperature: control it for at least thirty-six hours in anyone who doesn't respond to verbal commands, at a goal anywhere from thirty-two to thirty-seven point five degrees.

[[The pressure floor is sixty-five. The saturation is ninety to ninety-eight, the CO2 is thirty-five to forty-five, and temperature control lasts at least thirty-six hours.]]

And one line residents forget. Survivors with a suspected cardiac cause should have coronary angiography before they leave hospital, particularly after a shockable rhythm, unexplained left ventricular dysfunction, or severe ischaemia.

Before discharge is one thing. But who needs the cath lab tonight?

p12.question: After ROSC: the first hours
p12.bridge: The lungs are set. Now the pressure, where one keyed answer departs from every guideline.
p12.lesson:
The lungs first, because they are set within minutes of ROSC and they control two of the five targets.

Two airway steps begin it. Secure the airway if the patient is not protecting it. And pass a gastric tube. During CPR the bag and mask filled the stomach with air, as you saw in the first section, and a distended stomach splints the diaphragm and invites aspiration.

Then ventilate protectively, with a tidal volume of about six to eight millilitres per kilogram of predicted body weight. These lungs have often aspirated, they have been compressed, and they are now being reperfused. Lung injury is common after arrest.

Then the two gases.

Carbon dioxide is held at thirty-five to forty-five, normal. Check it on a blood gas instead of trusting the capnograph, and check it again whenever the temperature changes. A cooled patient makes less carbon dioxide. Leave the ventilator as it was, and he drifts into a low carbon dioxide without anyone touching a dial.

Oxygen is held at a saturation of ninety to ninety-eight per cent. The lower limit moved in twenty twenty-five. It was ninety-two before, and the European guideline still says ninety-four. What allowed the wider range was the BOX trial, which compared a lower and a higher oxygen target in comatose survivors and found the same outcome with both. So the safe zone is broad, and the harm is at the two ends.

[[After ROSC ventilate to normal: arterial carbon dioxide thirty-five to forty-five, saturation ninety to ninety-eight per cent. Hyperventilation, hyperoxia and hypoxia each injure the brain by a different route.]]

Name those routes, because the exam asks what to avoid. Hyperventilation constricts the brain's vessels and also raises pressure in the chest, which lowers output. Hyperoxia adds free-radical injury. Hypoxia repeats the arrest in miniature.

The Grand Test asked it twice. A post-arrest patient on temperature management: which should be avoided? Fever, hypoxia, or hyperventilation? All of the above. Everyone got it. The wrong reasoning is that only fever matters during temperature control.

One discriminator, because you know another setting where hyperventilation is used. In a herniating brain, a short period of hyperventilation buys time by shrinking the blood volume in the skull. The brain after an arrest has the opposite problem. It is short of flow. So here hyperventilation is only harmful.

b The ventilation strategy
c The PaCO2 target
d The saturation target

- **Lung-protective ventilation**
- **Maintain PaCO₂ 35-45 mmHg**
- **Target saturation 90-98%** (PaO₂ 60-105 mmHg; AHA 2025)
- **AVOID HYPERVENTILATION and HYPEROXIA**

viva.question: What BP and oxygen targets after ROSC?
viva.bridge: SpO2 90-98%, PaCO2 35-45, lung-protective breaths; avoid both extremes. Next: why hyperoxia is harmful, and why not to go too low →
viva.lesson:
The respiratory plan has five parts, and each has a reason.

The airway is secured. Then decompress the stomach with a nasogastric or orogastric tube. Why? Minutes of bag and mask ventilation have filled it with gas. A tense stomach splints the diaphragm and invites aspiration.

Then lung-protective ventilation. These lungs have had compressions, perhaps aspiration, and a body-wide inflammatory response. Treat them as lungs at risk of ARDS, with a tidal volume of six to eight millilitres per kilo of predicted body weight.

Now the heart of the card. Carbon dioxide.

You know from neuroanaesthesia that CO2 is the tap on the cerebral vessels. Lower the PaCO2 and the vessels constrict. Raise it and they dilate. In a healthy brain you use that to your advantage. In this brain, both directions are dangerous. Hypocapnia constricts vessels in tissue that's already short of flow. Hypercapnia dilates them and adds volume to a brain that may be swelling.

[[Keep the PaCO2 between thirty-five and forty-five. Hyperventilation after ROSC is a second ischaemic insult that you deliver yourself.]]

And here's the trap, and it's a very natural one. After an arrest he has a metabolic acidosis. The pH is seven point one. The instinct is to turn up the ventilator and correct it. Don't. You'd be fixing a number on the gas and constricting the brain to do it. The lactate will clear as the circulation recovers.

Does a slightly high CO2 help, by opening the vessels? That was tested too. The TAME trial compared mild hypercapnia with normocapnia and found no difference. So, normal.

Then oxygen. A saturation of ninety to ninety-eight percent. Your card's answer line still says ninety-two, and its own note corrects it. Say ninety.

And the card ends with the two things to avoid, which are really the summary: hyperventilation and hyperoxia. Low CO2 and high oxygen. Both feel like generosity to the patient, and both injure.

Now the last piece, and the one the panel will press. Why is too much oxygen harmful? And if it is, why not simply aim low?

p12.question: After ROSC: the first hours
p12.bridge: Pressure is held. Now the first of the two questions: is there an artery to open?
p12.lesson:
Now the circulation, and you have the tools for this from the two shock packets. After an arrest all three numbers can be off at once. The pump is stunned. The squeeze is lost, because reperfusion dilates the vessels. And the filling may be low. So you find out which is failing before you treat.

The lines come first: an arterial line, because vasopressors are titrated minute by minute, and a central line to deliver them. Then two investigations. A twelve-lead ECG, for the infarct. And an echo, which tells you which number is wrong: a poor ventricle, a vigorous ventricle with low resistance, or an obstruction such as tamponade or a dilated right ventricle.

The treatment follows the finding. Fluid only if the patient is volume-responsive, in small boluses, reassessed each time. The old fixed load of twenty to thirty millilitres per kilogram has gone, because a stunned ventricle can't handle it and the injured lung takes it up. For the vasopressor, noradrenaline is the usual first choice, with dobutamine when the stunned pump is the problem. Neither guideline claims one agent is proven. Mechanical support, a balloon pump, an Impella or ECMO, is not routine. It may be considered in selected patients with refractory cardiogenic shock.

Now the target. A mean arterial pressure of at least sixty-five, with a urine output of half to one millilitre per kilogram an hour. The purpose is cerebral perfusion.

[[The post-arrest pressure target is a mean arterial pressure of at least sixty-five. The BOX trial compared sixty-three with seventy-seven and found no difference, so a higher target has no guideline support.]]

That brings us to a question only twenty-four per cent matched. A comatose patient on temperature management, day one, with a mean pressure of sixty-five despite fluids. Next step? The key was to raise the mean pressure above eighty. The reasoning sounds sensible: a brain without autoregulation should like a higher pressure. But it was tested. BOX, in twenty twenty-two, assigned comatose survivors to a mean of sixty-three or seventy-seven and found no difference in death or severe disability. Three other trials agreed. No guideline asks for eighty.

So how do you answer? If that exact stem returns, with those options, the bank's key is above eighty. On a question framed by a guideline, the target is at least sixty-five. The European wording is a mean above sixty to sixty-five.

One discriminator stops this number from blurring with others. A mean of eighty-five to ninety belongs to acute spinal cord injury. Traumatic brain injury is managed by cerebral perfusion pressure. Neither applies after an arrest.

The other wrong options in that stem teach something too. 'Rewarm rapidly' causes rebound hypotension and fever. 'Stop temperature control because of a STEMI' is wrong, because the two run together. And 'delay reperfusion until he wakes' is wrong, for the reason on the next card.

[[After ROSC give fluid only if the patient is volume-responsive, noradrenaline first, and dobutamine for a stunned pump. Mechanical support is not routine.]]

viva.question: What BP and oxygen targets after ROSC?
viva.bridge: MAP above 65 with fluid, noradrenaline and echo, aimed at cerebral perfusion. Next: does aiming higher than 65 help →
viva.lesson:
First ask why he's hypotensive at all. The pulse is back, so why is the pressure soft?

Three reasons, and you met all of them a few minutes ago. The heart is stunned, so the pump is weak. The reperfusion response has dilated the vessels, like sepsis. And the capillaries are leaking, so the circulating volume is low. Pump, pipes and volume, all at once. It's cardiogenic shock and septic shock in the same patient.

So the plan has to look at all three.

You start with access and eyes. An arterial line, because you need the pressure beat by beat, and a central line. A twelve-lead ECG to look for infarction. And an echo, with a critical care ultrasound screen, to see what that ventricle is actually doing.

Then the targets. A MAP above sixty-five. A systolic above ninety. A urine output of half to one millilitre per kilo per hour.

[[The stated reason for the pressure target is cerebral perfusion. After an arrest, you are running the blood pressure for the brain.]]

That's the phrase the panel wants. Not for the kidneys, not for the cardiac output. For the brain.

Now how do you get there? Here I want to update the card. It gives a volume load of twenty to thirty millilitres per kilo of saline or Ringer's lactate. That's older teaching. A stunned ventricle tolerates a large fixed bolus badly. So the modern line is: give fluid only if he's fluid responsive, exactly as you learned in the shock package.

Then a vasopressor. Noradrenaline first. The card also lists adrenaline and dopamine, but noradrenaline is your first word. And if the echo shows that the weak pump is the main problem, add an inotrope.

If that fails, mechanical support. The card names three: the balloon pump, the Impella, and ECMO. The twenty twenty-five American guideline says temporary mechanical support may be considered in refractory cardiogenic shock after an arrest.

One encouraging point to hold on to. This stunning usually recovers over two to three days. So you are supporting a heart that's likely to come back.

So the floor is sixty-five. But if flow follows pressure, shouldn't a higher pressure mean a better-fed brain?

p12.question: After ROSC: the first hours
p12.bridge: The artery is dealt with. Now the brain begins to show its injury, and often the first sign is a jerk.
p12.lesson:
The first of the two questions: is there an artery to open?

Read the post-ROSC ECG. If it shows persistent ST elevation, the patient goes for emergent angiography, with PCI if a culprit is found. And the key phrase is 'comatose or not'. Coma is not a reason to wait.

That is where the Grand Test caught half the candidates. A man collapses in VF after shovelling snow. He has ROSC, his mental status can't be assessed, and the ECG shows a STEMI. When is angiography? Urgently, now. The wrong options were to wait for a favourable neurological prognosis, to correct the metabolic derangement first, and to go within twenty-four to forty-eight hours. Think about why waiting is wrong. You can't judge the brain's prognosis for at least three days. The muscle beyond the blocked artery dies in hours. And if the artery stays shut he may arrest again.

[[Persistent ST elevation after ROSC means emergent angiography, comatose or not. Temperature control starts alongside it and neither delays the other.]]

The NEET recall asked the same thing with instability added. VF arrest, ROSC, anterior ST elevation, unstable: immediate coronary angiography with PCI. The wrong option there is thrombolysis. Primary PCI is preferred, and prolonged or traumatic CPR raises the bleeding risk of a lytic. Lysis is kept for when PCI can't be reached in time.

Now the patient without ST elevation. This is where practice changed. It used to be argued that anyone resuscitated from VF with no obvious cause should go straight to the laboratory. Two trials tested that. COACT took about five hundred and fifty patients after a shockable arrest with no ST elevation. Survival at ninety days was sixty-five per cent with immediate angiography and sixty-seven with a delayed one. TOMAHAWK found no benefit either.

So without ST elevation, emergent angiography is reasonable only in three situations: cardiogenic shock, recurrent ventricular arrhythmias, or ongoing ischaemia. Otherwise it is not emergent, and it is done later, before discharge.

{{**Angiography after ROSC | When**
Persistent ST elevation (awake or comatose) | emergent
No STE + shock, recurrent VT/VF or ongoing ischaemia | emergent is reasonable
No STE, stable | delayed (COACT, TOMAHAWK)}}

[[Without ST elevation, immediate angiography adds nothing unless there is cardiogenic shock, recurrent ventricular arrhythmia or ongoing ischaemia. 'No obvious cause' is no longer an indication.]]

Two more lines on the card. Temperature control can be started during the angiogram, on the table. And the medical treatment for ACS, antiplatelets, anticoagulation and a statin, is begun in appropriate patients, adjusted for the bleeding risk that CPR leaves behind.

Finally the arrhythmias that follow ROSC. They are mostly secondary, so you treat the cause more than the rhythm: correct the potassium and magnesium, reperfuse the ischaemia, deal with any toxin, and correct the temperature. Cooling produces bradycardia. Rewarming and fever produce tachyarrhythmias.

**Give:**
a The five components of arrhythmia management post-arrest
b The four indications for coronary angiography
c When TTM can be initiated
d What else is started in appropriate patients
card.a:
- **Arrhythmias:** anti-arrhythmics • **correct electrolyte imbalance** • treat coronary ischaemia • **toxin management** • **temperature correction**
- **Emergent angiogram ± PCI (AHA 2025):** **persistent ST elevation**, comatose or not (COR 1) • reasonable without STE if **cardiogenic shock, recurrent ventricular arrhythmias or ongoing ischaemia** (COR 2a) • otherwise **not** emergent: no benefit over a delayed strategy (COR 3; COACT, TOMAHAWK)
- **TTM can be initiated DURING the angiogram**
- **ACS medical management** should be started in appropriate patients

viva.question: Post-cardiac-arrest care and temperature control.
viva.bridge: Emergent angiography for ST elevation, shock, recurrent VT/VF or ongoing ischaemia; not routine otherwise. Next: how cooling evidence changed →
viva.lesson:
Start with the logic. In adults, the commonest cause of a sudden arrest outside hospital is coronary disease. So for years the reflex was simple: ROSC, then cath lab, for everyone.

Two trials tested that reflex. COACT, from the Netherlands in twenty nineteen, took patients with a shockable rhythm and no ST elevation, and compared immediate angiography with a delayed one. TOMAHAWK, from Germany and Denmark in twenty twenty-one, did the same across all rhythms. Neither found any benefit from going immediately.

Why not? Think about who these patients are. Without ST elevation, an acutely blocked artery is uncommon. And these patients mostly die of the brain, not the heart. So an urgent trip to the cath lab fixes a problem most of them don't have, and delays the care for the problem they do.

So the twenty twenty-five rule has three tiers.

[[Emergent angiography for persistent ST elevation, whether he's comatose or awake. Reasonable without ST elevation if there is cardiogenic shock, recurrent ventricular arrhythmias or ongoing ischaemia. Otherwise, not emergent.]]

The first tier is a class one recommendation. The second is class two A. And the third is class three, no benefit, on the strength of those two trials.

The trap is the phrase no obvious cause. That used to be an indication. It no longer is.

The card carries three more points, and they're quick.

First, arrhythmias after ROSC. Don't just reach for amiodarone. Ask why the heart is irritable. Five things: give the anti-arrhythmic, correct the electrolytes, treat the coronary ischaemia, manage any toxin, and correct the temperature.

Second, temperature control does not wait for the cardiologist. It can be started during the angiogram. Coma is not a reason to delay the cath lab, and the cath lab is not a reason to delay the temperature control.

Third, if this was an acute coronary syndrome, start its medical treatment in the appropriate patients.

So the heart is dealt with. Now the brain. And the first thing we ever did for the brain was to cool it.

p12.question: After ROSC: the first hours
p12.bridge: You hold the current targets. The exam mixes them with the previous set, so put the two side by side.
p12.lesson:
This card is the first hours on one page, so check yourself against it.

Pressure: a mean of at least sixty-five. The card adds a systolic of at least ninety, which was the older pair. Gases: saturation ninety to ninety-eight, carbon dioxide thirty-five to forty-five. Temperature: thirty-two to thirty-seven point five, for any rhythm and any location, for at least thirty-six hours, with rewarming no faster than half a degree an hour. Angiography: at once for a STEMI, reasonable for shock, and not for everyone.

A Grand Test question you missed sits on the temperature line. The wrong options were a strict thirty-two to thirty-four degrees, excluding PEA from temperature control, and thirty-six degrees for twelve hours. Each is an old or an invented number. Any comatose survivor, any rhythm, at least thirty-six hours.

Now the one new item on this card, a definition. The EEG is watched in every patient who doesn't follow commands, and sometimes it shows seizures with no movement at all. When does that count as status epilepticus? When a seizure runs continuously for ten minutes or more, or when seizures occupy twenty per cent or more of any sixty minutes. That second half is twelve minutes in an hour.

[[Electrographic status epilepticus: a seizure lasting ten minutes or more continuously, or seizures filling twenty per cent or more of any sixty-minute period.]]

Marrow hangs three prognosis questions on this card, and they prepare you for the last section.

First: which finding in post-arrest coma is most specific for a poor outcome? Status epilepticus, or myoclonic status, during temperature control. It stands with the other poor signs: pupillary and corneal reflexes absent on both sides, a high neurone-specific enolase, and burst suppression on the EEG. All of them are read together, and not before seventy-two hours.

Second: a man is revived after a twenty-minute arrest, and you are asked which statement is not true. The false one is that no motor response in the upper limbs always means a poor outcome. Arms that are weak while the legs move can be a watershed injury, called man in a barrel. The border zones between the cerebral arteries are the last fields to be supplied when pressure falls, and the arm area of the motor cortex lies in one. It doesn't always mean a poor outcome.

Third: a brief arrest of three to five minutes can recover completely.

[[No single sign decides prognosis after arrest. Weak arms with moving legs may be a watershed injury, man in a barrel, and absent arm movement alone does not always mean a poor outcome.]]

viva.question: What BP and oxygen targets after ROSC?
viva.bridge: The injured brain has lost autoregulation, so pressure, CO2, oxygen and temperature all need a target. Next: the haemodynamic plan →
viva.lesson:
Start with the healthy brain, because you know this curve from neuroanaesthesia.

Across a wide range of mean arterial pressure, cerebral blood flow stays flat. When the pressure falls, the small arteries dilate. When it rises, they constrict. That's autoregulation. The brain protects its own flow, and you don't have to think about it.

After a cardiac arrest, that mechanism is damaged. In many patients the plateau is simply gone. In others it has moved to the right, so the brain now needs a higher pressure than before to hold its flow.

{{pic}}

On your screen, the solid line is the healthy plateau. The dashed line is the brain after arrest: a straight slope. Whatever the pressure does, the flow does.

[[After an arrest the brain is pressure-passive. Flow follows pressure. So every dip in blood pressure is a dip in brain blood flow, with no reserve to absorb it.]]

Now the rest of the card falls out of that one fact, in four short lines of reasoning.

Low pressure means more ischaemia. So you set a floor: a MAP of at least sixty-five, and a systolic of at least ninety.

Low CO2 constricts the cerebral vessels. So you keep the PaCO2 normal, thirty-five to forty-five.

High oxygen makes free radicals in reperfused tissue. So you aim for a saturation of ninety to ninety-eight percent, a PaO2 of about sixty to a hundred and five. One correction: your card says ninety-two to ninety-eight. The twenty twenty-five American figure is ninety to ninety-eight.

And fever means more neuronal death. So temperature control, thirty-two to thirty-seven point five, for at least thirty-six hours.

Two traps on this card, both of which have caught people in grand tests. First, a strict thirty-two to thirty-four degrees is outdated, and so is a short course: it's at least thirty-six hours. Second, temperature control is for every comatose survivor. Any rhythm, any location. A patient who arrested in PEA is not excluded.

The card also asks who goes for immediate angiography: ST elevation, or shock with a suspected coronary cause. Not everyone. And it defines electrographic status epilepticus, which you should be able to say: a seizure lasting ten minutes or more, or seizures filling a fifth or more of any hour of recording.

So the brain can't defend itself against low pressure. How do you defend it?

p12.question: After ROSC: the first hours
p12.bridge: You've met temperature control four times as a number. Section six is about where that number came from.
p12.lesson:
You now hold the targets of twenty twenty-five. The exam's favourite move is to offer you the previous set. So put them side by side.

{{**Target | AHA 2020 | AHA 2025**
Blood pressure | SBP ≥90, MAP ≥65 | **MAP ≥65** only
Temperature | 32–36 °C | **32–37.5 °C**
Duration | ≥24 h | **≥36 h**
SpO₂ | 92–98% | **90–98%**
PaCO₂ | 35–45 | 35–45}}

Take each change with its reason, because the reason is what makes it stay.

Pressure. The separate systolic target was dropped because the trials were all run on mean pressure. Four of them compared a mean of about sixty-five to seventy with a higher one, and found no benefit from the higher.

Temperature range. The top of the range rose from thirty-six to thirty-seven point five, first in a focused update of twenty twenty-three, after the TTM two trial showed that normothermia with fever prevention did as well as thirty-three degrees.

Temperature duration. The minimum rose from twenty-four hours to thirty-six, because the fever that follows early rewarming is linked to worse outcomes.

Oxygen. The floor fell from ninety-two to ninety, on the BOX result. Carbon dioxide didn't change. A trial of deliberately higher carbon dioxide showed no benefit.

[[What changed in twenty twenty-five: temperature control for at least thirty-six hours, not twenty-four; range up to thirty-seven point five, not thirty-six; saturation from ninety, not ninety-two; and mean pressure alone, with no systolic target.]]

The Grand Tests asked this twice. The most appropriate temperature strategy for a comatose patient after an arrest outside hospital: temperature control for at least thirty-six hours. The wrong options were at least twenty-four hours, strict hypothermia of thirty-two to thirty-four for seventy-two hours, and no temperature control unless seizures develop.

The second was an odd-one-out. Which is not a component of post-arrest care: a mean pressure of at least sixty-five, a carbon dioxide of thirty-five to forty-five, a temperature goal of thirty-two to thirty-five, or an EEG if not following commands? The answer is the temperature goal. Thirty-two to thirty-five belongs to no guideline. It was written to sit between the old range and the new one and look familiar.

[[A temperature goal of thirty-two to thirty-five degrees is in no guideline. The ranges that have existed are thirty-two to thirty-four, then thirty-two to thirty-six, and now thirty-two to thirty-seven point five.]]

Then the additions that are entirely new.

Imaging. A CT from head to pelvis, and an echo or bedside ultrasound, may be reasonable after ROSC. The CT finds the cause, such as a subarachnoid haemorrhage, a pulmonary embolus or a dissection, and it finds the injuries of CPR: broken ribs, a torn liver, a pneumothorax.

Glucose. Avoid both ends, below seventy and above a hundred and eighty milligrams per decilitre. There is no tighter target.

Myoclonus without an EEG correlate isn't treated, as you saw. Prognostication now looks for signs of a good outcome as well as a bad one, and a new blood marker has been added. Both wait for the last section.

And recovery. Survivors and their caregivers should have a structured assessment for anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress, with referral, before discharge.

viva.question: What changed in the 2025 AHA resuscitation guidelines?
viva.bridge: Post-arrest: MAP 65, SpO2 90-98%, temperature control 32-37.5 °C for at least 36 h. Next: the new prognostication points →
viva.lesson:
Post-cardiac arrest care is where the twenty twenty-five guideline changed the most, and it's the part you deliver, for days. Take it as a head-to-toe set of targets.

{{**After ROSC (AHA 2025)**
MAP ≥65 mmHg
SpO2 90–98% (PaO2 60–105 mmHg)
PaCO2 35–45 mmHg
Temperature control 32–37.5 °C for ≥36 h
Glucose 70–180 mg/dL}}

Blood pressure. A mean arterial pressure of at least sixty-five. Four randomised trials found no benefit from aiming higher.

Oxygen. A saturation of ninety to ninety-eight percent, with an arterial oxygen of sixty to one hundred and five millimetres of mercury. The carbon dioxide target is unchanged, at thirty-five to forty-five.

Temperature. This is the headline. Temperature control for at least thirty-six hours, with a goal anywhere between thirty-two and thirty-seven point five degrees. It used to be at least twenty-four hours, at thirty-two to thirty-six.

[[After the arrest: a mean pressure of at least sixty-five, a saturation of ninety to ninety-eight percent, and temperature control between thirty-two and thirty-seven point five degrees for at least thirty-six hours.]]

Notice the direction of travel. The target got warmer, and the duration got longer. Both a hypothermic strategy and a strategy of preventing fever now count as temperature control.

Then the rest. A CT from head to pelvis, and an echocardiogram, may be reasonable to find the cause. Keep the glucose between seventy and one hundred and eighty. Temporary mechanical circulatory support may be considered in refractory cardiogenic shock. And don't treat myoclonus unless there's a correlate on the EEG.

And the last link brings a duty. Before discharge, survivors and their caregivers should have a structured assessment for emotional distress, and referral.

That leaves the hardest decision in post-arrest care. When, and how, do you predict the outcome?

viva.question: What BP and oxygen targets after ROSC?
viva.bridge: AHA 2025 keeps MAP ≥65 because four RCTs found no gain from higher targets. Next: the biggest of them, BOX →
viva.lesson:
You met this card in the first group, as the summary of what changed in twenty twenty-five. For this question, one line of it matters.

The American guideline keeps the target at a MAP of at least sixty-five, and it gives the reason: four randomised trials found no benefit from aiming higher. The same card carries the oxygen change, a saturation of ninety to ninety-eight percent, and notes that the PaCO2 target of thirty-five to forty-five did not move.

So let's open the biggest of those four trials.

p12.question: Temperature control and shivering
p12.bridge: You know the target and where it came from. Now the practical conduct: the probe, the clock, and how it ends.
p12.lesson:
Now the trials, in order. There are four moments.

The first is two thousand and two. Two trials were published together, one from Europe and one from Australia, by Bernard. Both took comatose survivors of VF arrest outside hospital and cooled them to thirty-two to thirty-four degrees, for twelve to twenty-four hours. In the European trial a good outcome rose from thirty-nine per cent to fifty-five. In Bernard's it went from twenty-six to forty-nine. Hypothermia looked far better than no treatment, and thirty-two to thirty-four degrees became the standard.

Notice what the control patients got: nothing. Their temperature wasn't managed, and many of them developed fever. Hold that thought.

The second moment is twenty thirteen, the TTM trial. Nine hundred and fifty patients, thirty-three degrees against thirty-six, with temperature controlled in both arms. No difference. So the depth didn't seem to matter, and the guidelines widened to a constant thirty-two to thirty-six.

The third is twenty twenty-one, TTM two. About nineteen hundred patients, thirty-three degrees against normothermia with active prevention of fever. Again no difference in death or function, and more arrhythmias with haemodynamic compromise in the cooled arm.

Now go back to two thousand and two. The early trials didn't compare cold with normal. They compared cold with fever. The benefit may have been the fever that was avoided.

[[Early trials: cooling to thirty-two to thirty-four beat no temperature management. TTM: thirty-six is as good as thirty-three. TTM two: thirty-three is no better than normothermia with fever prevention. What survives is that fever harms.]]

One trial runs the other way, and it explains why cooling is still allowed. HYPERION, in twenty nineteen, studied non-shockable arrests, and thirty-three degrees gave more good outcomes than thirty-seven, about ten per cent against six. It was a small difference in a modest trial. But it is why the range still reaches down to thirty-two, and why non-shockable rhythms are included.

So here is where the guidelines stand.

{{**Era | Target | Duration**
2002–2010 | 32–34 °C | 12–24 h
After TTM (2015, 2020) | constant 32–36 °C | ≥24 h
ERC–ESICM 2025 | prevent fever, ≤37.5 °C | 36–72 h
**AHA 2025** | **32–37.5 °C** | **≥36 h**}}

America calls all of it temperature control. A hypothermic target of thirty-two to thirty-four and a normothermic one of thirty-six to thirty-seven point five both qualify. What isn't allowed is fever. Europe says simply: actively prevent fever, at thirty-seven point five or below, for thirty-six to seventy-two hours, and don't actively rewarm a patient who is mildly cold on his own. The older European wording, fever above thirty-seven point seven for at least seventy-two hours, is from twenty twenty-one.

Now the keyed answers that belong to an era.

The target after a VF arrest outside hospital, keyed thirty-two to thirty-four: the answer of two thousand and two. Pick it when only historical ranges are offered. Marrow keys thirty-four degrees for a comatose survivor of VF. That lies inside today's American range, so it stands. In that same Marrow stem the brainstem reflexes were absent, and the point was that brain death can't be declared this early after an arrest.

And one key that rests on weak ground. Which statement about therapeutic hypothermia is correct? The key is 'delaying initiation increases mortality', and about half chose it. No randomised trial shows that faster cooling helps. The largest test of early cooling gave cold saline before hospital to more than thirteen hundred patients. It found no benefit, with more re-arrest and more pulmonary oedema. So routine prehospital cooling with cold fluid is not recommended. But in that question the other options were plainly false: that it is for all arrests, that it runs forty-eight hours, that shivering is harmless. So the key is the least wrong answer.

[[Routine prehospital cooling with rapid cold intravenous fluid is not recommended: no benefit, more re-arrest and pulmonary oedema. 'Delay increases mortality' is keyed only because the other options are worse.]]
