viva.question: Post-cardiac-arrest care and temperature control.
viva.bridge: Practice moved from cool deeply to do not let him get hot. Next: the trial that settled whether 33 °C helps →
viva.lesson:
This is a story in four acts, and if you tell it in order, the guideline writes itself.

Act one. In two thousand and two, two trials appeared together in the New England Journal. One from Europe, one from Melbourne. Comatose survivors of ventricular fibrillation were cooled to between thirty-two and thirty-four degrees. More of them survived with good brain function. Cooling became the standard of care, and we called it therapeutic hypothermia.

But look at the comparison group in those trials. It was labelled normothermia, but fever was not strictly prevented, and many of those patients ran warm. An injured brain left alone tends to run hot. So there were always two possible readings. Was it the cold that helped? Or was it the absence of fever?

Act two. Twenty thirteen, the TTM trial, led by Niklas Nielsen. This time both groups were tightly controlled, one at thirty-three, one at thirty-six. No difference. So the depth of cooling did not matter.

Act three. Twenty twenty-one, TTM2. Thirty-three degrees against normal temperature with fever actively prevented. Again no difference, and more arrhythmia in the cold group. We'll take that trial properly in a moment.

{{pic}}

Act four, the guidelines. On your screen, follow the bars from left to right. The cold target loses its special status, and one thing stays: the red zone at the top.

[[Practice moved from cool him deeply to do not let him get hot. The one principle that survived every trial is that fever is harmful.]]

Why is fever so damaging here? Because every degree raises the brain's demand for oxygen, in a brain whose supply is already fragile. Heat widens the gap between what the neurons need and what they get.

And notice how the name changed with the evidence. Therapeutic hypothermia. Then targeted temperature management. Now simply temperature control. The American guideline of twenty twenty-five says at least thirty-six hours, at any steady target from thirty-two to thirty-seven point five. The European guideline of the same year goes further: just prevent fever, at or below thirty-seven point five, for thirty-six to seventy-two hours.

One correction to hold. Your card also shows the European position from twenty twenty-one, with a constant thirty-two to thirty-six degrees. That's history now. Quote twenty twenty-five.

There's a small paradox in the American numbers. The target got warmer, but the duration got longer, from twenty-four hours to thirty-six. That makes sense once you see that the job is fever prevention. Fever doesn't stop at twenty-four hours.

Now, the trial that carried all of this.

p12.question: Will he wake? Prognostication
p12.lesson:
For twenty years prognostication looked in one direction. Every test was a search for evidence that the patient would do badly. The guideline of twenty twenty-five turns it round, and that is the first of five changes on this card.

One: there are now predictors of a favourable outcome. Three are the ones to know. A continuous EEG background without discharges, within seventy-two hours. A normal NSE. And a motor response of withdrawal or better. The American list also counts an MRI with no restricted diffusion at two to seven days. Each is weak evidence alone, and each is read with the other tests. But they let you argue for continuing, and not only for stopping.

Be careful with one thing that is left off that list. Preserved pupillary or corneal reflexes do not predict a good outcome. Many patients who keep them still do badly. Their absence counts against the patient. Their presence proves little.

Two: neurofilament light chain joins NSE as a blood marker, as you saw. Axons.

Three: the EEG now works in both directions. A continuous background with no epileptiform discharges means a working cortex. Burst suppression, or a suppressed background, off sedation at seventy-two hours or later, means the reverse.

[[New in twenty twenty-five: signs of a good outcome. A continuous EEG background without discharges, a normal NSE, or a withdrawal motor response may support recovery. Preserved pupillary or corneal reflexes do not.]]

Four: myoclonus with no EEG correlate is not treated.

Five is the timing, and it is the one the Grand Test asked. The impressions from all the tests are consolidated at seventy-two hours or more after the return to normothermia, and after sedatives have been stopped. Count from normothermia, not from the arrest.

The stem was a patient on day two of cooling, with absent corneal reflexes and no response to pain. What is the next step in prognostication? Wait at least seventy-two hours. Eighty-three per cent. Cold itself depresses the reflexes, and the sedatives are still circulating. The wrong options were to withdraw now, and to send an NSE to guide an immediate decision.

[[Day two, still cooled, with absent reflexes: wait. Prognosis is consolidated at least seventy-two hours after normothermia and off sedation. Cold and sedatives both make the brain look worse than it is.]]

That is the last card of the packet, and of the cardiology series. So go back to where the series began.

Shock one opened with a single idea. Every shock is one of three numbers failing: the filling, the pump, or the squeeze. For nine packets you have found the failing number and held it up while the cause was fixed. An infarct took the pump. A rhythm took the pump's timing. A drug took the pump or the squeeze. A full pericardium and a clot in the lung took the filling. A torn aorta took all of them in turn.

Cardiac arrest is the three numbers failing together. Nothing fills, nothing pumps, nothing squeezes. Now look at what you did in this packet, in those terms. Your hands became the pump. Adrenaline became the squeeze. Pushing the uterus aside, letting the air out of a tense chest, replacing lost blood: each of those gave the filling back. And the shock cleared the rhythm so the heart's own pump could return.

When it did return, the three numbers came back stunned, and you read them just as you did in the first packet. Only the judge had changed. It was no longer the lactate. It was the brain.

So that is cardiology, from the first failing number to the last question a family asks. Read the three numbers. Find the one that is failing. Support it. Fix the cause.

b The new serum biomarker
c The EEG finding supporting a GOOD outcome
d The rule on myoclonus

- **NEUROFILAMENT LIGHT CHAIN (NfL)** added as a serum biomarker

viva.question: What changed in the 2025 AHA resuscitation guidelines?
viva.bridge: Prognosis is multimodal, at 72 h or later, and now includes good-outcome predictors and NfL. Next: old numbers against new →
viva.lesson:
Neuroprognostication is the decision about whether a comatose survivor will wake. The twenty twenty-five additions change its character.

Until now, every prognostic test pointed one way. Each one was a predictor of a poor outcome, and so each one was an argument for withdrawal. The new guideline adds predictors of a favourable outcome.

[[Prognostication now looks in both directions. It includes predictors of a good outcome, so the assessment can argue for continuing, and not only for stopping.]]

The example to quote is the EEG. A continuous background without discharges, within seventy-two hours, supports a favourable prognosis, when it's read together with the other tests.

There's a new blood test. Neurofilament light chain, a structural protein of the axon, is added as a serum biomarker.

Myoclonus. Treatment to suppress it without an EEG correlate is not recommended. There's no evidence that the jerks themselves add to the brain injury.

And the timing principle, which protects the patient from an early, wrong decision. The approach is multimodal, and the impression is delayed: at least seventy-two hours from the return of circulation, or from achieving normothermia.

For this question, the line is: multimodal, late, and now in both directions.

Now the quick-fire round. Old number, new number.

viva.question: How do you prognosticate after cardiac arrest?
viva.bridge: 2025 added predictors of good outcome and NfL. Next: the 2025 ERC-ESICM algorithm with its favourable signs and timings →
viva.lesson:
You met this card in the first group, among the twenty twenty-five changes. Here's what matters for this question.

Until twenty twenty-five, every test pointed one way, towards stopping. The American guideline changed that by adding predictors of a favourable outcome. A continuous EEG background without discharges, within seventy-two hours, now supports a good prognosis when it's read with other tests. It added a new blood marker, neurofilament light chain. It said not to suppress myoclonus that has no EEG correlate. And it kept the timing principle: multimodal, and no earlier than seventy-two hours after normothermia.

So the assessment can now argue for continuing, not only for stopping. The European guideline built that into its algorithm.
